newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open little changed, thin trade seen.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open little changed, thin trade seen.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened little changed in light trading Monday as investors wound down for the end of the year. A thinly traded session was expected despite the release of U.S. economic data.
November leading indicators, released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, were up 0.1 percent. Existing U.S. home sales were set for release at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
The dollar was mixed overnight in Europe after having soared to a new 45-month high of 116.20 yen on Friday.
At 900 EST/1400 GMT, the 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged from Friday's level at 99-22/32 to yield 6.52 percent.
"There was no response to leading indicators, but there may be some to existing home sales," said Carol Stone, economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
"They provide more of a concrete indication of what's going on in the economy, she said.
Stone noted that leading indicators are always well anticipated as the components of the index are known ahead of time.
Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities LLC, noted that the bond market hasn't reacted to leading economic indicators in years.
"But we do have existing home sales today and new home sales tomorrow, both of which could move the market," Levenson said.
Volume has been very light thus far this session and with most institutional investors already sidelined for the rest of the year flows will likely remain subdued.
Levenson said home sales data may spark some price movement, even if no significant volume is generated.
The short end of the maturity spectrum has been bolstered in recent sessions as investors seek that sector's safety and liquidity ahead of the yearend.

"Most of the marginal gains we have seen so far really transpired overnight in London. The market has been supported by the strong U.S. dollar," said William Sullivan, director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
The continued sprint by the dollar, especially against the Japanese yen, has lured foreign investors into U.S. Treasuries, Sullivan said.
In light trade, ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 101-19/32, yielding 6.28 percent. The 30-year bond was up 5/32 at 99-21/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 100-7/32, yielding 6.07 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-30/32, yielding 5.78 percent.
Three-month bill rates were up four basis points to 5.01 percent. Six-month bill rates were down one basis point at 5.06 percent. Year bill rates were down one basis point to yield 5.17 percent.
